transcript: Emerald fennell’s version of the Wuthering Heights is sort of like The Great Gatsby musical on Broadway in that they're not necessarily faithful adaptations of the source material, but they are highly entertaining reimaginings. And yes, in those reimaginings, we have lost layers that added important context to those novels, like the queerness in The Great Gatsby and the racial layer of the wuthering heights. But losing those layers is sort of like losing the part of The Little Mermaid where Ariel sacrifices herself for a man who cannot love her back, which is arguably an important layer to the original fairy tale that many interpret as Hans Christian Andersen writing about himself being in love with his male friend who could not love him back and ended up marrying a woman. And yet nobody's mad at Disney for cutting that out of their version because that's not the story that they wanted to tell. And I do think part of that is that we studied. Many people at least studied Wuthering Heights and The Great Gatsby in school, and so many people got attached to these stories. And seeing a version that is so vastly different from your own interpretation is a little jarring. And the, the gut. The gut reaction is, oh, this isn't necessarily good, because this isn't how I imagined it. And I do think there is a larger conversation to be had about why Emerald Fennell didn't interpret Heathcliff as being a person of colour. When she read the novel. But I'm not necessarily mad about that layer being cut from the story. And the movie version is arguably more diverse than that original novel was. And that's the cool thing about the art of adaptation is that you really can't adapt something one to one, from one medium to another. So there's always going to have to be adjustments and changes, whether that's cutting or adding characters or removing or adjusting framing devices, cutting out entire plot points, re viewing a story through a completely different lens, like this version of Wuthering Heights arguably being from Cathy’s point of view as opposed to Nelly's point of view. And so it's really interesting to see how different creatives view these stories and what they interpret as the important aspects of those original source materials. And that's going to differ from person to person. And that's no more evident in the fact that I have seen people call Nelly and Linton the. The villains of Wuthering Heights, when I arguably see Heathcliff and Cathy as the villains of their own story. If you have to prescribe any villain to the story. And the beauty of all of these stories is that because they're in the public domain, you can kind of do whatever you want with them. And so if you're not getting the adaptation that you want to see, you are more than welcome to go out there and find the resources to create it. On your own. To create the wuthering Heights version that you want to see. Or to create the dark, gritty, queer adaptation of The Little Mermaid that I actually now really want.
